# ghax A minimalist, terminal-native agent written in Go that takes on a **shape** — a design partner, a spec implementer, a telemetry watcher — and runs as a well-behaved citizen of the [herdr](https://herdr.dev/) runtime. Disclaimer: This works for me -- that's the entire guarantee. Built with AI in the loop, so check your own biases before you love it or hate it on principle. Use at your own risk, fork freely, and don't @ me when it explodes. (But do drop me a note if it helps -- pay it forward.) > **Status: working, early.** The engine, three loop modes, provider adapters (local, OpenAI, > Anthropic, and an offline mock), the compiled-in tools, config/shapes, sessions, and the herdr > client are implemented and tested (`make test`). It has not yet been exercised against a wide > range of live models. See [VISION.md](./VISION.md) for the why and [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md) for > the how. > > Try it with no model backend at all: `make build && ./bin/ghax --provider mock -p "hello"`. --- ## The problem You end up wanting the same agent for very different jobs. One moment it should be a thinking partner reasoning through a design with a big model. The next it should grind a project to a written spec, unattended. Sometimes it shouldn't be coding at all — it should sit on a telemetry stream and react when something interesting happens. Those jobs want different prompts, tools, models, and rhythms, but the machine underneath them is the same: read input, build context, ask a model, run tools, loop. Most agents make you pick one job and one runtime. And when you run several at once — across a laptop, a build server, and an edge box — you lose track of which one is working, which is stuck, and which is done. ghax is one small binary that solves both. You give it a **shape** (config, not code) and it becomes the agent that job needs. And because it reports its real state to herdr, a fleet of shaped instances stays legible: herdr never has to guess what any ghax is doing. ## Why build this? Because the agent should run on **your** inference, not someone else's API. The premise: you run one or more inference servers — Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp, TGI — on a workstation, a GPU box, a DGX, or a small cluster, and you front them with [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/), which exposes a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint with model routing, fallback, aliases, key management, and usage accounting. ghax points at that one endpoint. That buys you: - **Traffic stays on your network by default.** ghax only ever talks to your LiteLLM endpoint. Nothing leaves your network unless *you* wire an external backend into LiteLLM — and that is a single, deliberate config change in one file, not a decision scattered across every agent. - **One place for config, keys, routing, and monitoring.** Point a whole fleet of ghax agents at a single LiteLLM: model choices, provider keys, routing and fallback, budgets, rate limits, and usage logging all live there. You configure and observe every agent from one control point. - **No per-token cost and no rate limits** you did not set yourself — for anything served locally. - **The same agent everywhere.** One static Go binary, from an edge SBC to a Kubernetes pod, all talking to the same gateway. Most agents assume a hosted cloud API, a heavyweight runtime, or a plugin marketplace. ghax assumes you own the inference and want a small, inspectable, scriptable tool that takes on whatever shape the job needs — and stays legible when you run a fleet of them under herdr. It descends from [hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax) and keeps its restraint; [VISION.md](./VISION.md) records the full rationale and the deliberate omissions. ## Why this and not hax, pi, or OMP? These are the neighbors. Short version: **ghax is hax's philosophy in Go, with a first-class observe mode and herdr citizenship, built to point at your own LiteLLM-fronted inference.** **vs [hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax)** — hax is the direct ancestor, and ghax keeps almost all of it: one small binary, local-first, inspectable, no plugins / MCP / permission prompts, presets. What ghax changes: - **Go, not C.** One statically cross-compiled binary for the whole spectrum — edge SBC → server → Kubernetes pod — with goroutines and `context` instead of hand-rolled threads. Same footprint discipline, less ceremony. - **A first-class observe loop.** hax is request/response only; it can't sit on a telemetry stream and react. ghax's `observe` mode (sources → triggers → bounded reactions) is a peer of the REPL. - **herdr-native.** ghax ships authoritative status hooks, a screen manifest, and shape/model metadata so a fleet is legible; hax is just a well-behaved Unix tool. - **Shapes select the loop mode**, not only the prompt/model — so one binary is a REPL, a script step, or a watcher. If you only want coding at the terminal, in C, with no watcher and no fleet, use hax — it's the smaller, more proven thing. ghax is for when you also want the observe mode, herdr fleet visibility, and Go's one-binary reach across your hardware. **vs pi and OMP (oh-my-pi)** — these are richer, batteries-included agents with **package ecosystems** ([pi.dev](https://pi.dev/) packages) and full TUIs, and they're first-class herdr citizens too. ghax goes the other way on purpose: - **No package runtime, plugin ABI, or marketplace.** Extension is config, `SKILL.md`, and external CLIs — the hax stance. Less power, far less surface to audit, version, or break. - **One small static binary, not a platform.** Nothing to install beyond the binary; nothing dynamic to load at runtime. - **Shaped for non-coding jobs too.** The same engine watches telemetry or processes a stream, not only writes code. - **Citizen, not conductor.** ghax reports state to herdr but does not orchestrate peers or host a plugin surface — orchestration stays outside the process. If you want the ecosystem — installable packages, a plugin surface, a full-screen TUI — reach for pi or OMP. ghax is for when you want the *smallest* thing that can be many shapes, runs on your own inference, and stays legible in a fleet. The common thread: **you own the inference (LiteLLM in front of your servers), you want one auditable binary, and you want it to become whatever shape the job needs.** ## What it is - **One static Go binary.** Cross-compiles for servers, SBCs, and edge devices. Small footprint — it leaves the RAM for your models. - **Your inference, via LiteLLM.** Point ghax at a LiteLLM proxy fronting your inference server(s) (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp). One OpenAI-compatible endpoint, many models; `type: local` auto-discovers the served model. Cloud APIs work too, but self-hosted is the assumption. See [Model backend](#model-backend-litellm-in-front-of-your-inference). - **Three loop modes.** `interactive` (a REPL), `oneshot` (`-p`, clean stdout, resumable — the Unix seam for scripts), and `observe` (a long-running, event-driven watcher). - **A herdr citizen.** Reports authoritative status (`working`/`idle`/`done`) and rich metadata over the herdr socket, ships a screen manifest as a fallback, and resumes cleanly. It does not orchestrate other agents — that stays outside the process. - **Minimalist and inspectable, on purpose.** No MCP, no plugin ABI, no marketplace, no per-command permission prompts. Extend it with external CLIs, skills, and config. See [VISION.md](./VISION.md#9-non-goals) for what it deliberately omits and why. ## Model backend: LiteLLM in front of your inference ghax speaks the OpenAI-compatible chat API and is designed to point at a **LiteLLM proxy** that fronts one or more inference servers. Run a whole fleet of ghax agents against a single LiteLLM: ```mermaid flowchart LR g1["ghax · design-partner"] --> lite g2["ghax · spec-implementer"] --> lite g3["ghax · telemetry-watcher"] --> lite lite["LiteLLM proxy
models · keys · routing · budgets · usage"] lite --> ollama["Ollama"] lite --> vllm["vLLM / TGI / llama.cpp"] lite -. you configure this .-> cloud["cloud API
(Anthropic, Ollama Cloud, …)"] ``` LiteLLM is your **single control point**: it is the one place to add models, hold provider keys, set routing and budgets, and watch usage across every agent. **Traffic never leaves your network unless you add an external backend there** — a deliberate, auditable change in one file, not something any individual ghax decides. Point ten agents at one LiteLLM and you configure and monitor all ten from that one place. Configure a provider pointed at your LiteLLM endpoint. `type: local` auto-discovers the served model from `/v1/models`, so the common case is just a base URL: ```json { "default_provider": "dgx", "providers": { "dgx": { "type": "local", "base_url": "http://dgx:4000/v1", "model": "local-qwen", "params": { "temperature": 0.7, "top_p": 0.8, "top_k": 20, "repetition_penalty": 1.05 } } } } ``` `params` are passed through verbatim, so backend-specific sampling controls (Ollama's `top_k`, `repetition_penalty`) reach the model through LiteLLM. Per-response token usage flows back too, so `/usage` works on local models. ghax is not *locked* to LiteLLM — because it is an OpenAI-compatible client you can point it straight at Ollama, llama.cpp, or a cloud API (`openai` / `anthropic` provider types). But the assumed deployment, and the one the defaults and docs are written for, is LiteLLM fronting your own inference. ### How LiteLLM routes by model name ghax always sends the request to the **one** LiteLLM endpoint; the `model` name in the request is the routing key. ghax's own `provider` (`dgx`) only means *"talk to LiteLLM"* — it is **not** the upstream provider. LiteLLM looks the model name up in its `model_list` and the matching entry decides the backend: ```yaml # litellm config.yaml — the routing table model_list: - model_name: local-qwen # the alias ghax asks for litellm_params: model: ollama_chat/qwen3-coder-next # provider prefix "ollama_chat" -> Ollama api_base: http://localhost:11434 - model_name: claude # alias litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 # provider prefix "anthropic" -> Anthropic api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY # the key lives HERE, not in ghax ``` The backend is chosen from the **provider prefix** on `litellm_params.model` (the part before the `/`): `anthropic/…`, `openai/…`, `ollama/…`, `gemini/…`, `bedrock/…`, `azure/…`, or `openai/…` with a custom `api_base` for any OpenAI-compatible server. `api_base` says where, `api_key` says with what. The flow: ghax `POST /v1/chat/completions {"model":"claude", …}` → LiteLLM matches `claude` in the `model_list` → translates the OpenAI request into that backend's native API → calls it (with the key LiteLLM holds) → translates the response back to OpenAI shape for ghax. ghax sent only `"model": "claude"` and never knew Anthropic was behind it. So picking a model in ghax (`--model claude`, or a shape's `model`) is just choosing a `model_name` LiteLLM knows. Two things LiteLLM adds at this layer, invisibly to ghax: several `model_list` entries sharing one `model_name` get **load-balanced / failed over**, and you can declare `fallbacks` (e.g. `claude → local-qwen` on error). ## Prerequisites - Go (recent stable) to build the binary. - A model endpoint: a **LiteLLM proxy fronting your inference server(s)** (the assumed setup), or directly an OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoint. The offline `mock` provider needs nothing. - Optional: [herdr](https://herdr.dev/) if you want fleet visibility and persistent sessions. ## Quick start ```sh # Build the single binary. make build # -> ./bin/ghax # No model needed — the offline mock provider echoes, to prove the loop works. ./bin/ghax --provider mock -p "hello ghax" # Interactive, against your configured LiteLLM endpoint (model auto-discovered). ghax # One prompt, clean stdout — the scripting seam. ghax -p "list the TODOs in this repo" printf "explain main.go" | ghax -p # Run under a named shape. ghax --shape design-partner ghax --shape spec-implementer -p "implement the spec in docs/DESIGN.md" # An observe agent watching a stream and reacting. tail -F /var/log/telemetry.jsonl | ghax --shape telemetry-watcher # Continue or resume a session. ghax -c # continue the latest session for this directory ghax --resume # pick a past session ``` ## Configuration Configuration is plain text under the XDG config directory. Every setting has a canonical key and, where it makes sense, an environment variable. Resolution order, most explicit wins: **CLI flag > environment variable > saved runtime selection > config file default.** A **shape** is a named config bundle — loop mode, provider, model, effort, system prompt, tool profile, `skills` (`SKILL.md` directories composed into the system prompt), and (for observe shapes) sources and triggers. Shapes are files you keep in a repo. `effort` maps to the backend's reasoning control (`reasoning_effort` / extended `thinking`) for reasoning-capable models. A top-level `compact_at` token estimate enables automatic history compaction (default 12000; `0` disables; the `/compact` command works regardless). A shape's `system` prompt may be inline text or loaded from a file with the `FILE:` prefix (`"system": "FILE: ./prompts/coder.md"`); a named file that is missing is an error. See [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md#7-configuration-and-shapes) for the format and the full setting reference. **Project instructions.** ghax automatically loads the `AGENTS.md` hierarchy: on each run it walks up from the working directory (stopping at the repo root / home), collecting every `AGENTS.md` and appending them to the system prompt, nearest-wins. Disable with `"auto_instructions": false`. ### Example shapes Ready-to-copy configs live in [`examples/`](./examples/) — run one with `GHAX_CONFIG=examples/ ./bin/ghax` (from the repo root; see [examples/README.md](./examples/README.md)): | Config | Shape(s) | Demonstrates | | --- | --- | --- | | [`coding-agent.json`](./examples/coding-agent.json) | `coder` | The basic one — an interactive coding agent, full tool set, `system` prompt from a file (`FILE:`). | | [`design-partner.json`](./examples/design-partner.json) | `design-partner`, `coder` | Use a paid cloud model only for the thinking-heavy role: `design-partner` asks LiteLLM for the `claude` model (`effort: high`, read-only) while `coder` stays on the free local model — no API key in ghax; the key lives in LiteLLM. | | [`telemetry-watcher.json`](./examples/telemetry-watcher.json) | `watcher` | An `observe` shape that watches stdin and reacts only to lines matching `error/fail/critical/panic`. | | [`reviewer-with-skill.json`](./examples/reviewer-with-skill.json) | `reviewer` | A one-shot reviewer that loads a `SKILL.md` (a Go review checklist) into its system prompt. | A shape is just a block in the config: ```json "shapes": { "coder": { "loop": "interactive", "system": "FILE: examples/prompts/coder.md", "tools": ["read", "write", "edit", "bash", "task"] } } ``` **Interactive UI.** On a terminal, `ghax` clears the screen and renders a styled REPL: a header box (model · provider · shape · status), a boxed prompt, streamed responses, and a keybinding footer. Type `/help` for commands — `/clear` (fresh conversation), `/compact` (summarize history), `/usage` (session token totals), `/copy` (last response to clipboard), `/session`. `Ctrl-C` interrupts the current turn (not the program); `Ctrl-D` exits. When output is piped it falls back to a plain prompt so scripts are unaffected. `NO_COLOR` disables styling; `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1` forces it (e.g. piping into `less -R`). ## Common tasks | Task | How | | --- | --- | | Choose the model/provider | Config `default_provider`/`model`, or the `--provider` / `--model` flags. | | REPL commands | `/help` lists them: `/clear`, `/compact`, `/usage`, `/copy`, `/session`. | | Run a shape unattended, bounded | `ghax --shape -p ""` with `max_turns` set in the shape. | | Watch a stream and react | An `observe` shape with a source and a trigger; pipe or configure the source. | | Drive a loop from a script | Wrap `ghax -p` / `ghax -c -p` in a shell loop (the composition seam). | | Inspect what was sent/received | The transcript and trace outputs; sessions are plain files. | | Run in a fleet | Launch shaped instances under herdr; status and metadata report automatically. | ## Project structure See [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md#3-package-layout) for the authoritative layout. ``` ghax/ cmd/ghax/ entrypoint + flag dispatch internal/agent/ core loop, item log, turn state machine (pure) internal/provider/ provider adapters: local, openai, anthropic, mock, sse internal/tool/ compiled-in tools: read, write, edit, bash, task internal/observe/ observe loop: sources, triggers, reactions internal/herdr/ herdr socket client + status reporting + manifest internal/config/ config + shape resolution internal/session/ resumable session persistence internal/terminal/ styled-output helpers (color, boxes, screen control) internal/app/ wiring + the three drivers internal/cli/ flag parsing internal/skill/ SKILL.md loading into the system prompt examples/ ready-to-copy config examples + prompt files + a sample skill VISION.md DESIGN.md README.md ``` ## herdr integration ghax is built to be the best-behaved citizen on the herdr runtime: authoritative state reporting, correct semantics for the observe loop (a quietly-watching agent reads as `idle`, not a hung `working` pane), rich shape/model metadata, and clean session resume. It consumes herdr; it does not orchestrate peers through the socket. Details in [VISION.md](./VISION.md#7-herdr-integration-the-best-behaved-citizen-on-the-runtime) and [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md#8-herdr-client). ## Documentation - [VISION.md](./VISION.md) — what ghax is for and the principles that constrain it. - [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md) — the architecture, packages, interfaces, and testing strategy. ## License MIT. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

# ghax

**A minimalist, terminal-native, shape-shifting agent written in Go — a first-class citizen of the [herdr](https://herdr.dev/) runtime.**

Vision document. Date-stamped 2026-09-12. This is a north star, not a spec. It describes what
ghax is for, the principles that constrain it, and the architecture those principles imply. It
does not commit to APIs or timelines.

---

## 1. The thesis

One agent binary. Many jobs. The job changes; the machine underneath does not.

An agent instance might be a **thinking partner** reasoning through a design with a foundation
model. Another might be a **spec implementer** grinding a project to a written specification.
Another might not be coding at all — it might sit on a **telemetry stream**, watching for
something interesting and reacting ad hoc. Each of those looks different from the outside. Each
wants a different system prompt, a different tool set, a different model, a different rhythm.

But the thing running underneath is the same: read input, build context, ask a model, dispatch
tools, loop. The **shape** differs; the fundamental capabilities do not.

ghax is that underlying thing — small, inspectable, one static binary — plus a disciplined way to
give it a shape. It descends directly from [hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax), a
minimalist C coding agent, and it inherits hax's restraint on purpose. It adds three things hax
does not have, because our world needs them:

1. **Go.** Real concurrency, one cross-compiled binary, and a language that runs everywhere we
   deploy — from an Orange Pi at the edge to a Kubernetes pod.
2. **A first-class observe loop.** Not every useful agent is request/response. Some watch.
3. **Deep herdr citizenship.** When many shaped instances run at once, the runtime that herds
   them needs to know exactly what each one is doing, without guessing.

---

## 2. Lineage: what we keep from hax, what we change

hax earned its shape by saying no. We keep almost all of it and change three things.

### Kept

| hax principle | Why it survives in ghax |
| --- | --- |
| One binary, tiny footprint | An edge node has little RAM; leave it for the model. Go gives us the single binary; we defend the footprint. |
| Local models are first-class | Start a local server, point ghax at it, it discovers the model. Cloud is a config change, not a different product. |
| Respect the terminal | Stream Markdown and live tool output, preserve scrollback, never seize the terminal. |
| Inspectable | You can always see exactly what was sent to the model and what came back. Sessions and traces are plain files. |
| Extensibility from substrates already present | Config, Markdown files, and subprocesses — not a plugin ABI, not a marketplace. |
| Composes as a Unix tool | One-shot mode with clean stdout is the seam. Orchestration lives *outside* the process, where it can be versioned and tested. |
| No permission prompts | An in-process approval gate is not a security boundary. Isolation comes from the OS (container/VM). Restraint comes from the prompt and from bounded runs. |

### Changed

1. **C → Go.** hax hand-rolls threads, cleanup labels, and a JSON parser to stay lean. Go gives
   us goroutines, channels, `context.Cancellation`, and a standard library for free, and still
   compiles to one static binary. The footprint discipline stays; the ceremony goes.

2. **Request/response only → request/response *and* observe.** hax is a REPL: a turn is a
   round-trip. ghax keeps that and adds a peer: a long-running, event-driven loop that reacts to
   a stream. Same engine underneath (see §4).

3. **Runtime-agnostic → herdr-native.** hax is a well-behaved Unix tool and stops there. ghax is
   also a well-behaved Unix tool, but it additionally ships the hooks and the manifest that make
   it a *model-authoritative* citizen of herdr, so a fleet of shaped instances is legible at a
   glance (see §7).

### "Like pi, but in Go" — resolved

pi is small, ships first-class local models, and can be pointed at many jobs. That is the part we
want. We do **not** want pi's package/plugin runtime. ghax's answer to "add a capability" stays
pure hax: a CLI with a README, a skill that tells the model when to reach for it, or a
config-defined provider. See §6 and §9.

---

## 3. The core idea: one engine, many shapes

A **shape** is a named, versioned bundle that configures the engine for a job. It is a
config artifact, not code. A shape names:

- a **loop mode** — `interactive`, `oneshot`, or `observe`;
- a **provider + model + effort** — local or cloud, small or large;
- a **system prompt** — base and append, inline or from a file;
- a **tool profile** — which of the compiled-in tools are enabled, plus any external tools;
- optional **skills** and **project instructions** to load;
- optional **observe sources and triggers** (observe mode only).

Shapes are the same mechanism hax calls *presets*, widened to also select the loop mode and
observe wiring. Because a shape is just config, it is versionable, diffable, and shareable, and
it can live in a repo next to the code it works on.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Engine["ghax engine (one binary)"]
        core["agent core:\ncontext → model → tools → loop"]
    end
    A["shape: design-partner\ninteractive · big cloud model\nreasoning tools, no write"] --> core
    B["shape: spec-implementer\noneshot · coding model\nfull tool set, spec loaded"] --> core
    C["shape: telemetry-watcher\nobserve · small local model\nstream source + triggers"] --> core
    core --> H["herdr\n(authoritative status per instance)"]
```

Three example shapes, one binary, three very different jobs. herdr sees three legible citizens.

---

## 4. Architecture

### 4.1 The turn, unchanged

The heart is hax's loop, ported and kept honest:

```
input → build context → provider streams events → assemble turn → dispatch tools → loop
```

- The canonical conversation state is a **flat, provider-independent item log**. Compaction
  appends a summary seed; it never destroys history. Model-visible windows are built from the log,
  not by slicing it.
- **Provider adapters** own native API wire formats and emit provider-independent stream events.
  Agent behavior never depends on the shape of a provider's JSON.
- The **turn state machine** is pure: stream events in, owned conversation items out. No I/O, no
  terminal, no presentation. It is testable without a network or a TTY.
- **Frontends** (interactive REPL, one-shot, observe) supply presentation and cancellation
  through hooks. They do not each re-implement the continuation loop.

These are the stable seams. Everything below plugs into them.

### 4.2 Two loop modes over one core

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Shared["shared agent core (pure, testable)"]
        turn["turn state machine"]
        log["item log + compaction"]
        prov["provider abstraction"]
        tools["tool dispatch"]
    end

    subgraph RR["request/response driver"]
        repl["interactive REPL"]
        once["one-shot (-p)"]
    end

    subgraph OB["observe driver"]
        src["source: tail a stream\n(stdin, file, socket, http, exec)"]
        trig["trigger: match / threshold / schedule"]
        react["reaction: run a bounded user-turn"]
    end

    RR --> Shared
    OB --> Shared
    src --> trig --> react --> Shared
```

**Request/response** is hax's world: a user (or a script, or another process) supplies a prompt;
the engine runs a user-turn until the model stops asking for tools; the answer is printed.
Interactive and one-shot are two frontends over the same core.

**Observe** is the new peer. An observe shape declares one or more **sources** (a log tail, a
message socket, an HTTP long-poll, the stdout of a subprocess), one or more **triggers** (a
pattern match, a threshold, a debounce window, a schedule), and a **reaction** (a bounded
user-turn with its own prompt template). The driver waits on sources, evaluates triggers, and
when one fires it runs a normal, bounded user-turn through the *same* core. Go's concurrency is
what makes this natural: sources are goroutines feeding a channel; `context` cancels a reaction
cleanly; a running reaction can be pre-empted or debounced without special machinery.

The observe loop is deliberately **event-driven, not a busy poll**, and every reaction is
**bounded** (`max_turns`, timeout) so an unattended watcher cannot run away. It is the same
restraint hax applies to unattended one-shot runs, extended to a loop that may run for days.

Why this belongs in the core rather than in an outside script: the value is *reacting with the
agent's full context and tools* to something happening in real time, and reporting that reaction
as first-class status to herdr. A shell `while` loop around `ghax -p` cannot hold conversation
state across reactions, cannot express a debounce cleanly, and cannot tell herdr "I am watching
and idle" versus "I am reacting now." An observe agent can.

### 4.3 Providers: local and cloud are the same thing

A provider is an adapter behind one interface. The catalog spans the full range:

- **Local, same machine** — a local inference server (llama.cpp-style, Ollama-style). ghax
  auto-discovers the served model and its capabilities, as hax does. No config block needed for
  the common case.
- **Local network** — the same adapters pointed at another host on the LAN (a box with a GPU).
- **Cloud, OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible** — including hosted local-model clouds (e.g. Ollama
  Cloud) and aggregators (OpenRouter-style).
- **Config-defined endpoints** — a static endpoint variant is a config block reusing a protocol
  family, never a new Go shim.

The rule that makes shapes work: **the model backend is orthogonal to the shape.** A
telemetry-watcher can run a tiny local model on the same SBC it is watching; a design-partner can
run a large cloud model. Same binary, same engine, same tool contract — only the provider config
differs. "The shape may differ but the agent's fundamental capabilities don't" is enforced here.

Resolution order follows hax: an explicit CLI flag beats an environment variable beats a saved
selection beats the config default. The more explicit the input, the higher it wins.

### 4.4 Tools: a small compiled core, extended the hax way

A tiny set of tools is compiled into the binary and always available:

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | Read a file (or a slice of one). |
| `write` | Create or overwrite a file. |
| `edit` | Exact-match, surgical edits. |
| `bash` | Run a command; stream and cap its output. |
| `task` | Spawn a bounded sub-run under a named shape (a subagent role). |

That is the floor, and for many shapes it is the ceiling. Everything beyond it follows hax's
philosophy exactly — **there is no plugin ABI, no MCP client, no embedded scripting runtime, and
no marketplace.** A new capability is one of:

1. **An external CLI with a README.** The model already knows how to run a program, read its
   help, and recover from its errors. A skill tells it *when* to reach for one. The capability
   stays usable outside ghax — by you, by scripts, by other agents.
2. **A skill** — a `SKILL.md` directory that documents a workflow or a tool and is loaded on
   demand.
3. **A config-defined provider or shape** — for model/endpoint variation.

This is a real constraint and we mean it. It keeps the binary small, keeps capabilities
inspectable and portable, and keeps ghax honest about what it is. When something seems missing,
the questions, in order, are: can a project-instructions line or a skill cover it? Can a script
around `ghax -p` cover it? Would it be used routinely rather than configured once? Only then does
it belong in the binary — as a feature, not as a framework for features.

### 4.5 Config, sessions, and state

- **Config** is plain text, XDG-placed, with a canonical key for every setting and a matching
  environment variable where it makes sense. Runtime selections (provider, model, effort, shape)
  are stored separately from the config file.
- **Sessions** are structured, resumable, plain-file persistence — continue the latest, resume a
  chosen one, resume a specific id in one-shot mode. Observe sessions persist their watch state so
  a restarted watcher resumes where it was.
- **Transcript** (model-facing context) and **trace** (redacted HTTP/SSE) are always available
  for inspection. Nothing about what ghax did is hidden.

---

## 5. Why Go

Go is not incidental; it is the reason ghax can be one product across our whole deployment
spectrum.

- **One static binary, cross-compiled.** `GOOS`/`GOARCH` produces a native binary for x86_64
  servers, aarch64 SBCs, and the players and edge boxes we run. No runtime to install, no shared
  libraries to chase. This directly serves the portability we need across embedded Linux, SBCs,
  edge players, on-prem servers, and Kubernetes.
- **Concurrency as a first-class tool.** The observe loop, streaming providers, capped tool
  output, and bounded subagents are all goroutines and channels with `context` cancellation.
  hax hand-builds a cooperative background-job system in C; we get it from the language.
- **A standard library that covers the wire.** HTTP, JSON, TLS, and Unix sockets are in the
  stdlib. The herdr socket client (§7) is `net.Dial` plus `encoding/json` over newline-delimited
  frames — no dependency.
- **Small, auditable dependency set.** The default answer to "just add a library" is still no.
  The stdlib does most of it; every added dependency is a permanent tax on build, port, and audit.

---

## 6. Extensibility, stated plainly

Because this is where agents accrete complexity, it gets its own section.

**In the binary:** the five core tools, the provider protocol families, the loop modes. That is
it. New tools and new providers are added to the binary only when they clear the bar in §4.4.

**Outside the binary, without touching Go:**

- **Shapes / presets** — config bundles that select loop mode, provider, model, prompt, and tool
  profile. Also serve as subagent roles for the `task` tool.
- **Skills** — `SKILL.md` directories a shape lists; their instructions are composed into the
  system prompt. (Progressive, load-when-relevant disclosure is a possible future refinement.)
- **Project instructions** — a hierarchy of instruction files that apply without being invoked.
- **External CLIs** — any program on `PATH`, driven through the `bash` tool.
- **Config-defined providers/endpoints** — for static endpoint variants.

**Composition happens outside the process.** Orchestration that would be a hook or a plugin
elsewhere is a script that drives `ghax -p`, where it is versioned, inspected, and tested like any
other program. The one-shot mode with clean stdout is that seam.

---

## 7. herdr integration: the best-behaved citizen on the runtime

[herdr](https://herdr.dev/) is "tmux for agents" — a runtime that owns agent terminals, keeps
them alive across disconnects and reboots, federates machines over SSH, and — crucially — tracks
what every agent is *doing* (`working`, `blocked`, `idle`, `done`). herdr detects most agents by
heuristics: process-name matching and a TOML **screen manifest** matched against the terminal's
bottom buffer. Heuristics are a fallback; **lifecycle hooks are authoritative.**

ghax's role is deliberately scoped: **be the best-behaved citizen herdr has, not an orchestrator
of other agents.** When you run a fleet of shaped ghax instances — a design-partner here, three
spec-implementers there, a telemetry-watcher on an edge box reached over SSH — herdr should never
have to *guess* what any of them is doing. ghax tells it, precisely, because ghax knows its own
state exactly.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph herdr["herdr runtime (unified view over SSH)"]
        view["one window · combined agent list\nevery pane: working / blocked / idle / done"]
    end

    subgraph m1["laptop"]
        g1["ghax · design-partner\nworking"]
    end
    subgraph m2["build server"]
        g2["ghax · spec-implementer\nblocked: needs a decision"]
        g3["ghax · spec-implementer\nworking"]
    end
    subgraph m3["edge SBC"]
        g4["ghax · telemetry-watcher\nidle: watching stream"]
    end

    g1 -- "authoritative state + metadata" --> view
    g2 -- "authoritative state + metadata" --> view
    g3 -- "authoritative state + metadata" --> view
    g4 -- "authoritative state + metadata" --> view
```

### 7.1 What "good citizen" means concretely

1. **Authoritative status, never guessed.** ghax detects the herdr environment (`HERDR_ENV`,
   `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH`, `HERDR_PANE_ID`) and reports its own state over the socket — `pane.report_agent`
   — at exactly the moments its internal state changes. herdr's heuristics become unnecessary for
   ghax panes. *Implementation note:* ghax self-reports `working`, `idle`, and `done`; it does not
   yet self-report `blocked` (nothing detects "needs a human decision" from inside a turn). herdr's
   own vocabulary still includes `blocked`, and the screen manifest lets herdr detect a
   blocked-looking pane heuristically (e.g. the model printing `proceed? (y/n)`).

2. **A screen manifest as a safety net.** ghax still ships a TOML detection manifest
   (`~/.config/herdr/agent-detection/ghax.toml`) so that even without the socket — an old herdr,
   a restricted runtime, a pane reattached before hooks are live — herdr classifies ghax panes
   correctly from the visible UI. Authoritative hooks first; manifest as fallback.

3. **Rich, legible metadata.** ghax publishes `pane.report_metadata` describing *which shape* it
   is (design-partner / spec-implementer / telemetry-watcher), which model and provider it is on
   (local vs cloud, small vs large), and a short task label. A fleet becomes readable at a glance:
   you can see that two implementers are on a local coding model and the watcher is on a tiny
   on-device model, without attaching to any of them.

4. **Correct state semantics for the observe loop.** This is where authoritative reporting earns
   its keep, because heuristics cannot infer it. An observe shape maps its lifecycle to herdr's
   vocabulary:

   | ghax observe state | herdr status |
   | --- | --- |
   | Watching sources, nothing firing | `idle` |
   | A trigger fired; running a bounded reaction | `working` |
   | Watch terminated (source closed / stopped) | `done` |

   A watcher that is quietly watching reads as `idle`, not as a hung `working` pane. When it
   reacts, it flips to `working` and back. herdr — and you — always know the difference. (A
   future `blocked` — "a reaction needs a human decision" — is not yet emitted; see the
   implementation note above.)

5. **Clean session state and live handoff.** ghax sessions are resumable plain files, which is
   exactly what herdr's session-restore, history-replay, and native-agent-resume expect. A ghax
   pane survives a herdr server restart and resumes its session; a live handoff hands over a real,
   inspectable conversation, not a black box.

### 7.2 Explicit non-goal: ghax does not drive other agents

herdr's socket API can spawn panes and prompt and wait on *other* agents (`pane.split`,
`agent.prompt`, `agent.wait`). ghax **consumes** herdr (reports state, reads its own context) but
does **not** reach across the socket to orchestrate peers. That restraint is deliberate and it is
consistent with hax's philosophy: cross-agent orchestration is composition, and composition lives
*outside* the process — in herdr itself, in a human driving the window, or in a script driving
`ghax -p` instances. Keeping ghax a citizen and not a conductor keeps the core small and keeps the
orchestration layer where it can be inspected and tested. (If this ever changes, it will be a
deliberate, separately-justified decision — not a quiet feature.)

---

## 8. The deployment spectrum

ghax is designed to be the same tool everywhere we work:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    edge["edge / SBC / player\ntiny local model\nobserve: telemetry watcher"]
    lan["workstation / GPU box\nlocal or LAN model\ninteractive: design partner"]
    server["on-prem / cloud server\ncloud or local model\noneshot: spec implementer"]
    k8s["Kubernetes\ncloud model\noneshot at scale"]

    edge -.->|ssh, one binary| herdr((herdr))
    lan -.->|local| herdr
    server -.->|ssh| herdr
    k8s -.->|jobs| herdr
```

- **Edge / SBC / player.** A tiny binary and a tiny local model leave the box usable. The
  observe shape watches a local telemetry stream and reacts on-device, reporting `idle`/`working`
  to a herdr instance reached over SSH.
- **Workstation.** Interactive design-partner and implementer shapes against local, LAN, or cloud
  models.
- **Server / Kubernetes.** One-shot shapes driven by scripts or jobs, at scale, with clean stdout
  and resumable sessions for the outer loop to build on. Containerize with podman.

One binary, cross-compiled. One config model. One engine. Different shapes.

---

## 9. Non-goals

Stated so "why doesn't ghax have X?" has an answer.

- **No MCP client or server.** A capability is a CLI with a README plus a skill. (§4.4)
- **No plugin ABI or embedded scripting runtime.** Extension is config, Markdown, and
  subprocesses. Go's lack of a stable dynamic-plugin story is a feature here, not a limitation.
- **No per-command permission prompts.** An in-process gate is not a security boundary; it trains
  reflexive approval. Isolation is the OS's job (container/VM); restraint is the prompt's and
  `max_turns`'s job.
- **No in-turn interception (hooks/vetoes on tool calls).** Composition lives outside the process.
- **No peer orchestration through the herdr socket.** ghax is a citizen, not a conductor. (§7.2)
- **No taking over the terminal.** Streaming output, preserved scrollback, nothing seized.
- **No marketplace.** Shapes and skills are files you keep in a repo.

---

## 10. Open questions

Deferred deliberately; each will get its own design pass.

1. **Observe source vocabulary.** Which sources ship in the core (stdin, file tail, exec stdout,
   Unix socket, HTTP long-poll) versus which are covered by piping an external CLI into a simpler
   source. Lean minimal; add only what is used routinely.
2. **Trigger expressiveness.** How much matching/threshold/debounce logic belongs in config
   before it should just be a small external classifier the model or a trigger shells out to.
3. **Subagent boundaries.** How the `task` tool's bounded sub-runs report to herdr — as child
   panes, as metadata on the parent, or invisibly.
4. **Compaction for long-lived observe sessions.** A watcher running for days needs a compaction
   policy tuned for "mostly idle, occasional reaction," not for a coding conversation.
5. **Manifest maintenance.** Keeping the ghax screen manifest in step with the REPL's actual UI
   as it evolves, so the fallback never lies.

---

## 11. Glossary

- **Shape** — a named, versioned config bundle that configures the engine for one job (loop mode,
  provider, model, prompt, tools, observe wiring). ghax's version of hax's *preset*.
- **Turn** — one provider round-trip: one assistant response plus optional tool calls.
- **User-turn** — one prompt (or one triggered reaction) plus every turn until the model stops
  requesting tools.
- **Loop mode** — `interactive`, `oneshot`, or `observe`.
- **Observe loop** — the event-driven driver: sources → triggers → bounded reaction, over the
  shared core.
- **Citizen** — an agent that reports authoritative state and metadata to herdr and resumes
  cleanly, but does not orchestrate other agents.
- **Manifest** — the TOML screen-detection file herdr uses to classify a pane's state as a
  fallback when authoritative hooks are unavailable.

---

## License

MIT. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

# ghax — Design

Detailed design for ghax. Read [VISION.md](./VISION.md) first for intent and non-goals; this
document is the how. Date-stamped 2026-09-12.

> **Status: implemented (early).** The design below is realized in code under `internal/`, verified
> by `make test`. Some signatures differ slightly from the original sketches (for example the
> model-visible context type is named `agent.Request`, and the `Provider`/`Tool` interfaces live in
> the `agent` package, at the consumer). The seams are as described.

---

## 1. Scope and status

This design covers the agent engine, the three loop modes, the provider and tool abstractions,
config and shapes, session persistence, and the herdr client. It fixes the package boundaries and
the interfaces that cross them. It does not specify wire-level JSON for each provider, nor the
exact config-file grammar; those are follow-on design passes noted in
[VISION.md §10](./VISION.md#10-open-questions).

Guiding constraints, from the user's engineering rules and hax's lineage:

- Idiomatic Go, standard-library-first, small auditable dependency set.
- Small, composable interfaces. The core is pure and testable without a network or a TTY.
- Errors are values and propagate; no defensive swallowing. Validate at boundaries with
  preconditions; fail loudly on violated invariants.
- One static binary. Concurrency via goroutines, channels, and `context.Context`.

## 2. Architecture overview

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph drivers["Loop drivers (frontends)"]
        repl["interactive REPL"]
        once["oneshot"]
        obs["observe"]
    end

    subgraph core["Agent core (pure)"]
        loop["agent loop"]
        turn["turn state machine"]
        log["item log + compaction"]
        ctx["context builder"]
    end

    subgraph adapters["Adapters (impure)"]
        prov["provider adapters"]
        tools["tools"]
        sess["session store"]
        herdr["herdr client"]
    end

    repl --> loop
    once --> loop
    obs --> loop
    loop --> turn
    turn --> log
    loop --> ctx
    ctx --> log
    loop -->|stream events| prov
    loop -->|dispatch| tools
    loop -->|persist| sess
    loop -->|status/metadata| herdr
```

The **core** owns conversation state and the turn state machine and knows nothing about HTTP,
terminals, sockets, or wall-clock time except through injected interfaces. **Drivers** supply
input and presentation. **Adapters** own the impure edges. The dependency arrows point inward:
adapters depend on core interfaces, never the reverse.

## 3. Package layout

```
ghax/
  cmd/ghax/                main(): flag parsing, wiring, driver selection
  internal/
    agent/                 core loop, item log, turn state machine, context builder
      item.go                struct item, item log, kinds
      turn.go                pure stream-event -> item state machine
      loop.go                continuation loop; driver hooks
      compact.go             summary-seed compaction
    provider/              provider abstraction + adapters
      provider.go            Provider interface, StreamEvent, Context types
      openai/                OpenAI + compatible (incl. hosted local clouds)
      anthropic/             Anthropic + compatible
      local/                 llama.cpp-style / ollama-style discovery
      config/                config-defined endpoint variants
      mock/                  scripted provider for tests
    tool/                  Tool interface + compiled-in tools
      tool.go                Tool interface, registry
      read.go write.go edit.go bash.go task.go
    observe/               observe loop: sources, triggers, reactions
      source.go trigger.go react.go
    herdr/                 herdr socket client + status/metadata reporting
      client.go status.go manifest.go env.go
    config/               config + shape resolution
      config.go shape.go resolve.go
    session/              resumable session persistence (plain files)
    terminal/             rendering, streaming, scrollback-preserving output
    cli/                  flag/env parsing shared by drivers
  docs/
```

`internal/` keeps the surface private; ghax is a program, not a library. Each package answers
"what does it do, how do you use it, what does it depend on" on its own.

## 4. The agent core

### 4.1 The item log

The canonical conversation state is a flat, provider-independent slice of items. It is the single
source of truth; every other representation (model context, display history, session file) is
derived from it.

```go
// internal/agent
type ItemKind int

const (
    ItemUserText ItemKind = iota
    ItemAssistantText
    ItemToolCall
    ItemToolResult
    ItemTurnBoundary // separates consecutive turns inside one user-turn
    ItemSummarySeed  // compaction output; never deletes prior items
)

type Item struct {
    Kind    ItemKind
    Text    string        // user/assistant text, or summary
    Call    *ToolCall     // ItemToolCall
    Result  *ToolResult   // ItemToolResult
    Meta    ItemMeta      // timestamps, token usage, provider tags — never read by the state machine
}

type Log struct { items []Item }

func (l *Log) Append(it Item)
func (l *Log) Items() []Item // read-only view
```

Compaction appends an `ItemSummarySeed` and marks earlier items as out-of-window; it never
mutates or removes history. The full log is always what gets persisted and inspected.

### 4.2 The turn state machine

`turn.go` is pure: borrowed stream events in, owned items out. No I/O, no presentation, no
goroutines. This is the most heavily unit-tested unit in the codebase.

```go
type StreamEvent struct {
    Kind  StreamEventKind // text-delta, tool-call-start, tool-call-args-delta, tool-call-end, usage, done, error
    Text  string
    Call  *ToolCallDelta
    Usage *Usage
    Err   error
}

// Turn folds a stream of events into the items produced by one provider round-trip.
type Turn struct { /* accumulator state */ }

func (t *Turn) Feed(ev StreamEvent) error // advance; error on protocol violation (precondition)
func (t *Turn) Done() (assistant Item, calls []ToolCall, err error)
```

A malformed event sequence is a precondition violation and returns an error; the turn does not
guess or paper over it.

### 4.3 The context builder

Model-visible context is built from the log, never by slicing it. The builder assembles the system
prompt (base + append + shape + project instructions), the in-window items, and any loaded skill
content, and hands the provider a provider-independent `Context`.

```go
type Context struct {
    System   string
    Items    []Item   // in-window items only
    Tools    []ToolSpec
}

func BuildContext(log *Log, sys SystemPrompt, tools []ToolSpec, win Window) Context
```

### 4.4 The loop and driver hooks

`loop.go` runs the continuation loop shared by all three drivers: build context, stream a turn,
append items, dispatch tool calls, repeat until the model stops requesting tools or a bound is
hit. Drivers inject presentation and cancellation:

```go
type DriverHooks struct {
    OnAssistantDelta func(text string)      // stream to terminal, or discard in oneshot
    OnToolCall       func(call ToolCall)     // show activity
    OnToolResult     func(res ToolResult)
    OnStatus         func(AgentStatus)        // -> herdr client (§8)
    Cancelled        func() bool              // Esc in REPL, ctx.Done() elsewhere
}

func Run(ctx context.Context, dep Deps, in UserInput, hooks DriverHooks) (Outcome, error)
```

`Deps` carries the injected `Provider`, tool registry, session store, and clock. A user-turn is
bounded by `max_turns` and a timeout carried on `ctx`. Cancellation is cooperative: a running turn
checks `ctx` and `Cancelled()` between events and between tool dispatches.

## 5. Providers

A provider adapter owns one native API family and nothing else. It serializes a `Context` to the
native request, opens the stream, and translates native wire events into `StreamEvent`s. Agent
behavior must never branch on a native response shape.

```go
// internal/provider
type Provider interface {
    // Stream runs one turn. It emits StreamEvents on the channel and closes it when done.
    Stream(ctx context.Context, c agent.Context, opts Options) (<-chan agent.StreamEvent, error)
    // Model returns the active model's name and provider, for display.
    Model() ModelMeta
}
```

- **Discovery.** The `local` adapter queries a local/LAN inference server for its served model and
  capabilities so the common case needs no config block (hax's behavior).
- **Cloud and compatible.** `openai` and `anthropic` adapters cover their families and their
  compatibles, including hosted local-model clouds and aggregators, via base-URL + auth config.
- **Config-defined variants.** A static endpoint variant is a config block that selects a protocol
  family and overrides base URL / headers — not a new Go type.
- **Usage, not in the adapter.** Adapters translate the provider's `usage` counts into
  `agent.Usage`; token accounting is accumulated by the loop (`Outcome.Usage`) and the app
  (`/usage`), not computed in adapters.
- **Effort and sampling params** are applied here: `reasoning_effort` / `thinking` from
  `Options.Effort`, and the provider's `params` map merged into the request body.

Transport (HTTP/SSE mechanics, retries, redaction for traces) is shared, using `net/http` and the
standard library; adapters own only protocol translation. Both translation and transport are
testable in isolation — the `mock` provider replays scripted events with no network.

## 6. Tools

A tool is a small interface. The compiled-in set is fixed (`read`, `write`, `edit`, `bash`,
`task`); everything else is an external CLI driven through `bash`, per
[VISION.md §4.4](./VISION.md#44-tools-a-small-compiled-core-extended-the-hax-way).

```go
// internal/tool
type Tool interface {
    Name() string
    Spec() ToolSpec                 // JSON schema advertised to the model
    Run(ctx context.Context, args json.RawMessage, env Env) (Result, error)
}

type Env struct {
    Cwd    string
    Stdout io.Writer   // for streaming/capped output
    Limits Limits      // output cap, timeout
}
```

- `bash` streams and caps output, classifies commands, and enforces a timeout. It is the seam for
  every external capability.
- `task` spawns a bounded sub-run under a named shape (a subagent role), reusing `agent.Run` with
  its own `Deps` and a fresh log. How sub-runs surface to herdr is an open question
  ([VISION.md §10](./VISION.md#10-open-questions)).
- Enabled tools are selected by the shape's tool profile; a tool absent from the profile is not
  advertised to the model.

Tools validate their arguments as preconditions and return errors; they do not silently coerce
bad input.

## 7. Configuration and shapes

Two layers: **config** (durable settings, plain text under XDG) and **runtime selections**
(provider/model/effort/shape chosen interactively, stored separately). Resolution, most explicit
wins:

```
CLI flag  >  environment variable  >  saved runtime selection  >  config file default
```

A **shape** is a named bundle:

```go
// internal/config
type Shape struct {
    Name       string
    Loop       LoopMode          // interactive | oneshot | observe
    Provider   string
    Model      string
    Effort     string
    System     SystemPrompt      // base + append, inline or @file
    Tools      []string          // enabled tool names
    Skills     []string          // SKILL.md directories to load
    Instr      []string          // project-instruction files
    MaxTurns   int               // bound for unattended runs
    Observe    *ObserveConfig    // required iff Loop == observe
}
```

Shapes double as subagent roles for `task`. They are files kept in a repo, versioned and diffable.
The config format reuses one parser shared with anything else that needs structured data, to avoid
a second grammar (hax's one-format rule).

**System prompt from a file.** A shape's `system` (and the config's `system_base`) may be inline
text or a `FILE:`-prefixed path (`"system": "FILE: ./prompts/coder.md"`); the named file is read in
its place. A missing file is an error — a shape that points at a prompt file requires it to exist.
Ready-to-copy examples live in `examples/`.

**Project instructions (`AGENTS.md`).** On every run, `composeSystem` walks up from the working
directory collecting `AGENTS.md` files and appends their contents to the system prompt,
outermost-first so the nearest (most-specific) file wins. The walk stops at the repository root (a
directory holding `.git`), the home directory, or the filesystem root, and never reads above home.
It is on by default; set `"auto_instructions": false` to disable. This is the automatic counterpart
to a shape's explicit `instructions` list.

**Skills.** Each entry in a shape's `Skills` is a `SKILL.md` directory (or the file itself). At
prompt-assembly time `internal/skill` loads each one — parsing its `name`/`description` frontmatter
— and `composeSystem` appends a `# Skills` section carrying their full instructions to the system
prompt. A listed skill that is missing is an error.

**Effort.** A shape's (or `--effort`'s) reasoning level is carried on `Options.Effort` and sent to
the backend: the OpenAI adapter sets `reasoning_effort`; the Anthropic adapter maps it onto extended
`thinking` with a budget and raises `max_tokens` to fit. It is opt-in and only meaningful for
reasoning-capable models.

**Sampling params.** A provider's `params` map is merged verbatim into each request body (protected
structural keys excepted), so temperature, `top_p`, `top_k`, `repetition_penalty`, and other
backend-specific controls pass through — including via a LiteLLM proxy. Applied by the OpenAI and
Anthropic adapters.

**Auto-compaction.** A top-level `compact_at` (a rough window token estimate) wires
`Deps.Summarizer` + `Deps.CompactAt`; when the window exceeds it the loop summarizes history into a
seed before the next turn. `0` disables it; the manual `/compact` command works regardless.

## 8. herdr client

The herdr client makes ghax a model-authoritative citizen. It is a thin package over a Unix
socket, with the standard library only.

### 8.1 Environment detection

On startup the client reads the herdr environment: `HERDR_ENV`, `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH` (falling back
to the documented default and `HERDR_SESSION` resolution), and the context ids `HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID`,
`HERDR_TAB_ID`, `HERDR_PANE_ID`. If `HERDR_ENV` is unset, the client is a no-op and ghax runs as a
plain terminal tool.

### 8.2 Transport

Newline-delimited JSON over the socket, one object per line, request/response by `id`:

```go
// internal/herdr
type request struct {
    ID     string          `json:"id"`
    Method string          `json:"method"`
    Params json.RawMessage `json:"params,omitempty"`
}
type response struct {
    ID     string          `json:"id"`
    Result json.RawMessage `json:"result,omitempty"`
    Error  *rpcError       `json:"error,omitempty"`
}
```

`net.Dial("unix", path)` on Unix; the named-pipe equivalent on Windows. Failures to reach herdr
are logged and swallowed *only here*, at this integration edge — a missing runtime must never take
down the agent.

### 8.3 Status reporting

The client maps the core's `AgentStatus` onto herdr's vocabulary via `pane.report_agent`, called
exactly on state transitions (driven by `DriverHooks.OnStatus`):

```go
type AgentStatus int
const (
    StatusIdle AgentStatus = iota // REPL awaiting input; observe watching
    StatusWorking                  // running a turn / a triggered reaction
    StatusDone                     // oneshot finished; observe watch terminated
)
```

ghax self-reports `idle`, `working`, and `done`. It does **not** currently self-report `blocked`
(nothing detects "needs a human decision" from inside a turn), so that state is not in the enum.
herdr's own vocabulary still includes `blocked`, and the screen manifest (§8.5) lets herdr detect a
blocked-looking pane heuristically — for example the model printing a `proceed? (y/n)` prompt.

For the observe loop this is what heuristics cannot infer: a quietly-watching agent reports
`StatusIdle`, not a hung `working` pane. See [VISION.md §7.1](./VISION.md#71-what-good-citizen-means-concretely).

### 8.4 Metadata

On startup and on shape change, the client publishes `pane.report_metadata` with the shape name,
provider/model (and local-vs-cloud, size class), and a short task label, so a fleet is readable
without attaching.

### 8.5 Screen manifest

A TOML detection manifest ships in-repo and installs to
`~/.config/herdr/agent-detection/ghax.toml`. It matches ghax's visible REPL states so herdr
classifies ghax panes correctly even when the socket is unavailable. The manifest is a fallback;
authoritative hooks win. Keeping it in step with the REPL UI is a maintenance item
([VISION.md §10](./VISION.md#10-open-questions)).

### 8.6 Non-goal

The client reports and reads; it never calls `pane.split`, `agent.prompt`, or `agent.wait` to
drive other agents. Peer orchestration lives outside the process
([VISION.md §7.2](./VISION.md#72-explicit-non-goal-ghax-does-not-drive-other-agents)).

## 9. The observe loop

The observe driver runs sources, triggers, and reactions over the shared core.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Source (goroutine)
    participant D as Observe driver
    participant T as Trigger
    participant C as Agent core
    participant H as herdr client

    D->>H: status = idle
    loop watching
        S->>D: event
        D->>T: evaluate(event)
        alt trigger fires
            D->>H: status = working
            D->>C: Run(reaction user-turn, bounded)
            C-->>D: outcome
            D->>H: status = idle
        else no fire / debounced
            D->>D: keep watching
        end
    end
```

```go
// internal/observe
type Source interface { // stdin, file tail, exec stdout, unix socket, http long-poll
    Events(ctx context.Context) (<-chan Event, error)
}
type Trigger interface { // match / threshold / debounce / schedule
    Fire(ev Event) (react bool, prompt string)
}
```

- Sources are goroutines feeding one channel; the driver selects over them and `ctx.Done()`.
- Each reaction is a normal bounded user-turn (`MaxTurns`, timeout) so an unattended watcher can
  never run away.
- Reactions can be debounced or pre-empted; a new firing while a reaction runs is coalesced per
  the trigger's policy.
- Observe sessions persist watch state so a restart resumes the watch, not just the conversation.

The source and trigger vocabulary is deliberately minimal at first; anything exotic is an external
classifier shelled out to via `bash`.

## 10. Concurrency model

- One foreground goroutine owns the loop and the item log; the log is not shared across goroutines.
- Providers stream on a channel the loop consumes; the provider goroutine exits when the stream
  closes or `ctx` cancels.
- Observe sources are goroutines feeding a channel; the driver owns the fan-in.
- The `task` tool runs a sub-run with its own `Deps` and log; inputs are copied, not shared.
- `context.Context` carries cancellation and deadlines everywhere. Every spawned goroutine is
  joined before the state it touches is torn down. No global mutable state beyond process config
  resolved once at startup.

## 11. Error handling

- Errors are values and propagate up to the driver, which decides presentation. The core does not
  log-and-continue.
- Boundaries (tool args, provider events, config, socket frames) validate with preconditions and
  return errors on violation. Invariants that "cannot" break use explicit checks, not silent
  fallback.
- The single exception is the herdr integration edge (§8.2): a missing or broken runtime is
  logged and swallowed so the agent still runs standalone.

## 12. Sessions and persistence

Sessions are structured, resumable, plain files (JSONL-style item records plus a small header),
keyed by working directory. `-c` continues the latest; `--resume` picks one; `--resume=ID -p`
resumes a specific session in one-shot mode. Observe sessions additionally persist watch state.
Transcript (model-facing context) and trace (redacted HTTP/SSE) are separate inspection outputs,
never substitutes for the session file.

## 13. Testing strategy

- **Pure core, no network, no TTY.** The turn state machine, item log, compaction, and context
  builder are unit-tested directly. Table-driven tests for event folding, including malformed
  sequences that must error.
- **Mock provider.** `provider/mock` replays scripted stream events so the full loop, tool
  dispatch, and observe reactions run hermetically.
- **Tool tests** run against temp directories; `bash` classification and output capping are tested
  without spawning long processes where possible.
- **herdr client** is tested against an in-test Unix socket that speaks the newline-JSON protocol
  and asserts the exact `pane.report_agent` / `pane.report_metadata` calls and their timing.
- **Interactive REPL** needs a real tty; drive it with tmux (send keys, capture pane), scoped to a
  named session — never `killall`.
- No test is skipped or stubbed to make a run pass; a failing test is a failing build.

## 14. Build and tooling

- `make build` produces `./bin/ghax`; `make test`, `make lint` are the gates. Builds go through the
  Makefile, not ad hoc `go build`.
- Cross-compilation targets (via `GOOS`/`GOARCH`) for x86_64 and aarch64 servers, SBCs, and edge
  devices are Makefile targets.
- Dependencies are standard-library-first; each addition is justified and auditable.
- Containers use podman.

## 15. Security and isolation

- Isolation against a mistaken or compromised run comes from the OS: run ghax in a container or VM
  when working on untrusted input or when blast radius matters. There is no in-process permission
  gate, by design ([VISION.md §9](./VISION.md#9-non-goals)).
- Restraint comes from the system prompt (forbid destructive git, ask before irreversible actions),
  Esc-to-steer in the REPL, and `max_turns` on unattended runs.
- Secrets (API keys) come from the environment or config marked secret; they are never written to
  sessions and are redacted in traces.

## 16. Design decisions

Date-stamped; each records a choice and its reason.

- **2026-09-12 — Go over C.** One static cross-compiled binary plus real concurrency and a wire-
  capable stdlib, keeping hax's footprint discipline without hand-rolled threads and parsers.
- **2026-09-12 — Observe as a first-class loop, not a script.** Reacting with full context and
  tools, and reporting accurate `idle`/`working` to herdr, cannot be expressed by a shell loop
  around `-p`.
- **2026-09-12 — herdr citizen, not conductor.** ghax reports authoritative state and metadata and
  resumes cleanly, but does not drive peers over the socket; orchestration stays out of process.
- **2026-09-12 — Pure hax extension stance.** Five compiled-in tools; everything else is external
  CLIs, skills, and config. No MCP, no plugin ABI, no marketplace.

# ghax — Design Seed

**What it is:**  
A minimalist, Go-written terminal agent with three loop modes (`interactive`, `oneshot`, `observe`), one static binary, shaped via config. Runs on your inference (LiteLLM fronting local/cloud models), reports authoritative state to [herdr](https://herdr.dev/), and is a first-class runtime citizen.

**Key architecture:**
- **Core (pure):** `internal/agent/` — item log, turn state machine, context builder
- **Adapters (impure):** `internal/provider/`, `internal/tool/`, `internal/herdr/`, `internal/session/`, `internal/observe/`
- **Drivers (frontends):** `cmd/ghax/` — REPL, oneshot, observe loop

**Loop modes:**
- `interactive` — REPL (streaming output, `/help` commands, `Ctrl-C` to interrupt)
- `oneshot` — `-p "prompt"`, clean stdout, resumable sessions
- `observe` — event-driven watcher (source → trigger → bounded reaction), reports `idle`/`working` to herdr

**Provider support:** `local` (auto-discover model), `openai`, `anthropic`, `mock`, config-defined variants. Points at LiteLLM by default.

**Tools (compiled-in):** `read`, `write`, `edit`, `bash`, `task`

**Extensibility (outside binary):** shapes (config bundles), `SKILL.md`, `AGENTS.md` project instructions, external CLIs via `bash`.

**Shape = config bundle:** loop mode, provider/model/effort, system prompt (inline or `FILE:`), tools, skills, observe wiring (sources/triggers/reactions), bounds (`max_turns`).

**herdr integration:**  
Reports `pane.report_agent` (`idle`, `working`, `done`) and `pane.report_metadata` (shape, model, task label) over Unix socket. Screen manifest as fallback.

**Build:** `make build` → `./bin/ghax`. Tests: `make test`.

**Status:** implemented, early — engine, providers, tools, shapes, sessions, herdr client, tests pass. Not yet exercised widely against live models.

**Where it diverges from hax (C ancestor):**
- C → Go (goroutines, context, stdlib HTTP)
- `observe` loop (event-driven watching)
- herdr citizenship (authoritative status/metadata)
- Same restraint: no plugins, no MCP, no marketplace; extension via config/Markdown/CLI.

**Non-goals (per VISION.md §9):** no MCP, no plugin ABI, no permission prompts, no peer orchestration through herdr socket, no terminal takeover.
